Write the Methods Paragraph for a Fitted Mixture Model

Source: R/report_methods.R
report_methods.Rd

Returns the paragraphs a methods section needs to describe a fitted model: the sample, the estimator and its random starts, missing data, the fit indices, classification quality, any structural model, and the line of R that refits it. Every number is read off the fitted object, so the text is true of the fit it was written from and of no other.

Usage

report_methods(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'mixture_model'
report_methods(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'lta_model'
report_methods(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'mixture_comparison'
report_methods(object, k = NULL, ...)

Arguments

object

A fitted model (fit_mixture(), fit_gmm(), fit_lcga(), fit_rmlca(), fit_lta()) or a comparison from compare_mixtures() or compare_longitudinal().

...

Unused.

k

For a comparison only: the number of classes of the model the paragraphs describe. Default is the comparison's lowest-BIC model.

Value

A character vector of class methods_report, one paragraph per element, with the cited works in attr(, "references"). Printing it wraps the paragraphs and lists the references.

Details

Why this exists. Sorgente et al. (2025) coded 313 latent class analyses published in psychology between 2014 and 2024 against the published tutorials: 23% reported the estimator, 16% the random starts, 17% how missing data were handled, and 1.6% their analysis code. Every one of those items is a value the package already stores; this function puts them in the order and the wording a methods section uses.

What it does not do. It reports and never grades. No sentence calls an entropy, a class size or a replication count adequate: where the literature attaches a cutoff, the cutoff is discussed in the help page that computes the number (for entropy, compare_mixtures()). It does not say why the number of classes is substantively right, what the classes mean, or whether the sample suits the question; those are the author's.

Passing a comparison (from compare_mixtures() or compare_longitudinal()) adds the enumeration paragraph: the range of K, whether the one-class model was in it, the indices reported, and which K had the lowest BIC. The other paragraphs then describe the model with k classes, by default the lowest-BIC one.

Citations are returned as the references attribute and printed once at the end, so the paragraphs serve both in-text and numbered citation styles.

References

Sorgente, A., Caliciuri, R., Robba, M., Lanz, M., & Zumbo, B. D. (2025). A systematic review of latent class analysis in psychology: Examining the gap between guidelines and research practice. Behavior Research Methods, 57, 301.

Masyn, K. E. (2013). Latent class analysis and finite mixture modeling. In T. D. Little (Ed.), The Oxford Handbook of Quantitative Methods (Vol. 2, pp. 551-611). Oxford University Press.

Weller, B. E., Bowen, N. K., & Faubert, S. J. (2020). Latent class analysis: A guide to best practice. Journal of Black Psychology, 46(4), 287-311. doi:10.1177/0095798420930932

Nylund-Gibson, K., & Choi, A. Y. (2018). Ten frequently asked questions about latent class analysis. Translational Issues in Psychological Science, 4(4), 440-461. doi:10.1037/tps0000176

See also

grolts_report() for the trajectory-model checklist.

Examples

set.seed(1)
X <- matrix(rbinom(600, 1, 0.5), nrow = 100)
fit <- fit_mixture(X, n_classes = 2, measurement = "binary", n_init = 5,
                   random_state = 1)
report_methods(fit)
#> The analysis sample comprised 100 cases. Classes were defined by 6
#> binary indicators.
#> 
#> A 2-class latent class model was estimated by maximum likelihood with
#> the EM algorithm (Dempster, Laird, & Rubin, 1977), with weak priors
#> that keep estimates off the boundary of the parameter space (Galindo
#> Garre & Vermunt, 2006): 1 pseudo-observation for the class proportions
#> and 1 pseudo-observation for the item-response probabilities. The
#> search used 5 random starts; the best log-likelihood was reached by 5
#> of them. The algorithm converged in 180 iterations.
#> 
#> The model's log-likelihood was -405.31 with 13 free parameters (AIC =
#> 836.62, BIC = 870.49, sample-size-adjusted BIC = 829.43).
#> 
#> Relative entropy was 0.427. The smallest class held 34.7% of the sample
#> (about 35 cases). The average posterior probability of the assigned
#> class ranged from 0.758 to 0.839 across classes. These describe how
#> cleanly cases are classified; they are not criteria for the number of
#> classes (Masyn, 2013).
#> 
#> Models were estimated with the R package mixtureEM (version 0.6.0) in R
#> 4.6.1. Random starts were drawn with random_state = 1. The model is
#> refitted by: fit_mixture(indicators = X, n_classes = 2, measurement =
#> "binary", n_init = 5, random_state = 1)
#> 
#> References
#> Dempster, A. P., Laird, N. M., & Rubin, D. B. (1977). Maximum
#>   likelihood from incomplete data via the EM algorithm. Journal of the
#>   Royal Statistical Society: Series B, 39(1), 1-38.
#> Galindo Garre, F., & Vermunt, J. K. (2006). Avoiding boundary estimates
#>   in latent class analysis by Bayesian posterior mode estimation.
#>   Behaviormetrika, 33(1), 43-59. https://doi.org/10.2333/bhmk.33.43
#> Masyn, K. E. (2013). Latent class analysis and finite mixture modeling.
#>   In T. D. Little (Ed.), The Oxford Handbook of Quantitative Methods
#>   (Vol. 2, pp. 551-611). Oxford University Press.
